title: Clarity Can Be A Decision
author: Braincentric
summary: The author argues that clarity in working life is universally desired but chronically inaccessible because most people — and most AI tools — treat clarity as something found in more information, when the research on cognition shows it emerges from three sequential decisions made in a specific order. Drawing on the work of Wiggins and McTighe on backward design and the hard ceiling of working memory (which holds only a few moving pieces at once), the author and a cognitive neuroscientist developed a framework called the Nested Egg. The three decisions are: name what winning would look like (the measured outcome), identify the single Big Idea that carries the person there, and choose two load-bearing supports for that idea — cutting everything else ruthlessly. The article illustrates the framework with three unlikely historical examples — Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, Kennedy's moon-shot speech, and an Aesop fable — showing that the same three-decision structure underlies the most durable communications in human history. The article closes with an announcement of a live demonstration of the framework in August.
points: Clarity is not found in more information — AI accelerates the problem by delivering 'tonnage faster and piled neater,' burying the central question rather than answering it. The pile gets taller and the center gets harder to find.

The Nested Egg framework operates in a specific sequence: first name what winning looks like (the measurable outcome), then identify the one Big Idea, then select only two load-bearing supports. The order is non-negotiable because each decision constrains the next.

Working memory holds only a few moving pieces at once before the whole board goes blurry — which is why piling on more has always buried understanding instead of building it. The framework enforces the cognitive constraint that more will always violate.

Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, Kennedy's moon shot, and Aesop's tortoise-and-hare fable all run on the same three-decision structure — separated by twenty-five centuries and radically different topics, united by the same underlying architecture.

The three calls AI cannot make for you: what winning looks like for this specific person in this specific room on this specific day, which single idea matters most, and which two things carry it there. Machine stacking is the problem; human decision-making about what to cut is the solution.
quotes: Clarity is the most wanted thing in working life right now, and almost nobody can get a clean cup of it.

What the machine gives you is tonnage, delivered faster and piled neater than you could ever manage alone. More options, more angles, more confident paragraphs, all of it landing on top of the same question you walked in with. You feel busy. You feel covered. The pile got taller and the center got harder to find.
Real clarity gets built in a specific order, and the order is the whole game.

Lincoln stood at Gettysburg after the day's headline speaker had run two hours, and he spoke for two minutes. One Big Idea: the living must finish the work the dead began, so that government of the people, by the people, for the people does not perish. Two supports, the founding and the sacrifice. Around two hundred and seventy words, and we still carry them.

That is why clarity is a decision. Three of them, made on purpose and in order. What would winning look like. What is the one idea. What two things carry it there. Make those three calls and the fog lifts, the same way every time.

Those are the three calls the machine cannot make for you. It has no idea what your win looks like. It cannot feel which single idea matters most to you, in this room, on this day. Naming the win, the idea, and the two stays with you, and it always will.
